items.title: Google Summer of Code 2026 results
items.summary: The Rust Project participated in Google Summer of Code (GSoC) for the third time this year. This time we had 13 projects, and our dear contributors have been working very hard on them for several months. As usual, the projects had various durations, so while some of them have ended in August, the last one has only finished in November, so we have been waiting until we have all the results before publishing this blog post.We are very happy to announce that all 13 projects were successful and passed their final evaluation! We consider it to be a testament to the diligence of our contributors, and the helpfulness of our mentors, that we are able to keep a very high rate[1] of successful GSoC projects several years in a row.At the start of summer, we had a video call with our contributors, so that we could all get to know each other a bit, and learn about their projects. Over the following few months, we continuously communicated with the contributors, provided guidance and answered their questions and reviewed their pull requests. And most importantly, we learned many new things together! It was an overall great experience. We are grateful for all Rust contributions done by our GSoC participants and for the time we spent working together, and we hope that we will continue seeing at least some of them around in the future.We would like to thank all our Rust GSoC 2026 contributors. You did a great job!Even though this year we had fewer projects than in 2025, mostly due to limited mentoring capacity, Google Summer of Code 2026 was again a success for the Rust Project. We think that GSoC is a great way of introducing new contributors to our community, and we are looking forward to participating in GSoC (and other mentorship programs, such as Outreachy) again in the near future. If you are interested in becoming a (GSoC) contributor, check out our GSoC project idea list and our guide for new contributors.Below you can find a brief summary of our GSoC 2026 projects. You can find more information about the original goals of the projects here. For easier navigation, here is an index of the project descriptions in alphabetical order:A Frontend for Safe GPU Offloading in Rust by Marcelo DomínguezAdding WebAssembly Linking Support to Wild by Kei AkiyamaBringing autodiff and offload into Rust CI by Shota SuganoDebugger for Miri by Mohamed AliImplementing impl and mut restrictions by Ryosuke YamanoImproving Ergonomics and Safety of serialport-rs by Tanmaylibc: transition differing bit-width time and offset variants and deprecate bug-prone constants by Adam MartinezLink Linux kernel and its Modules with Wild by Vishruth ThimmaiahMigrating rust-analyzer assists to SyntaxEditor by bit-alooPort std::arch test suite to rust-lang/rust by Sumit KumarReorganizing tests/ui/issues by zedddieUtilize debugger APIs to improve debug info test accuracy and error reporting by Anthony BoldenXDG path support for rustup by Guicheng LiuAnd now strap in, as there is a ton of great content to read about here!A Frontend for Safe GPU Offloading in RustContributor: Marcelo DomínguezMentor: Manuel DrehwaldFinal reportMarcelo worked on improving the usability of cross-vendor GPU programs in Rust using the std::offload module. At the start of the project, the offload prototype was only a proof of concept. It assumed that the offloaded code was bug-free, and it required users to write a lot of boilerplate code. Marcelo resolved both issues over the summer.First, he implemented proper type checking. Marcelo extended the compiler to verify that the arguments passed to any offload call are of the correct type, as expected by the GPU kernel. Kernel launches are thus now safe.After that, he added support for generic kernels. The compiler now collects all generic instantiations launched from the CPU side, and loads that info later when compiling GPU kernels to make sure we instantiate them as needed. Marcelo also added support to select which GPU to use, which is helpful for laptops with both an integrated and a dedicated GPU, as well as for servers with multiple GPUs. He also added two macros that removed the need for any boilerplate when writing and launching GPU kernels.The hardest part of this project by far was dealing with references. Due to Rust semantics, we cannot just map types containing mutable references to GPUs and then process them using multiple threads. Previous Rust GPU projects used raw pointers as a workaround, but we obviously wanted to avoid those. Marcelo managed to implement a sound abstraction so that users can now safely declare how their kernels will access mutable arguments.As a cherry on top, Marcelo also ported the RajaPerf performance suite from C++ to Rust and used it to benchmark his pull requests. His safe Rust version matches the performance of the original C++ code, and is now described in a GPU offload paper that he is working on together with his mentor, Manuel.
